arXiv:cond-mat/0411094v2 [cond-mat.str-el] 02 Jun 2005

Quantized spin models

Sufficient Conditions for Topological Order in Insulators

M. B. Hastings Affiliation: Center for Nonlinear Studies and Theoretical Division, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM 87545, hastings@lanl.gov
November 1, 2004
Abstract

We prove the existence of low energy excitations in insulating systems at general filling factor under certain conditions, and discuss in which cases these may be identified as topological excitations. In the specific case of half-filling this proof provides a significantly shortened proof of the recent higher dimensional Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem.

pacs
75.10.Jm

The classic 1961 result of Lieb, Schultz, and Mattis (LSM)[1], proving the existence of an excitation within energy ∼1/L\sim 1/L of the ground state for certain one dimensional spin chains, has had a large effect on the field. While it was then proven by Affleck and Lieb[2] that one dimensional systems either have gapless localized excitations or a local symmetry breaking, it has long been suspected that in higher dimensions there is a more interesting possibility of topological order[3].

One way to understand topological order is based on flux insertion. We give the physical argument here, and then discuss the difficulties in this argument which give rise to the need for the more careful argument of this paper. We consider a higher-dimensional system which is periodic in one direction. A spin-1/21/2 system can be mapped to a hard-core boson system on a lattice, with the presence or absence of a particle denoting spin up or down. If the particle system is superfluid, there is long range order in the xx and yy components of the spin in the original system, implying the existence of low energy excitations. On the other hand, if the particle system is insulating, it should be possible to insert 2​π2\pi of gauge flux in the hopping of particles across a given line cutting the system, returning the Hamiltonian to the original one, but, for non-integer filling fraction, taking the system to an excited state which is very close in energy to the ground state. Using adiabatic flux insertion, this was suggested as a way to prove a higher dimensional LSM theorem[4]. The two possibilities would thus seem to be a superfluid system (or other system which resists flux insertion) which has low energy excitations, or an insulating system which has topological order. In either case, there is a state close in energy to the ground state.

However, there is a serious problem with this argument. The definition of adiabatic flux insertion depends on the existence of a gap (but does not require anything about the magnitude of a gap); however, in a spin system with no disorder, any gap in the spectrum at zero flux must close at some non-zero value of the flux, thus making it impossible even to define an adiabatic flux insertion[5]. In a fractional quantum Hall system with disorder, there is a related problem. In a 1/31/3 quantum Hall state, the gap between the three approximately degenerate ground states remains open for all values of the flux, even though the gap is exponentially small. However, this means that adiabatic flux insertion leaves the system in the lowest of the three states and does not produce the correct topologically excited state[6]. Thus flux must be inserted slowly, but not adiabatically. For fractional Hall systems, the experimentally relevant flux insertion is slow enough to avoid exciting states above the three almost degenerate ground states, but fast enough to “shoot through” the level crossing.

A precise definition of this quasi-adiabatic flux insertion was given in [7], and used to prove a version of the LSM theorem for spin systems with total Sz=0S^{z}=0 valid in arbitrary dimension. The flux was inserted in such a way that the ground state wave function was only disturbed near the flux insertion point. Physically, one can imagine that the flux was inserted sufficiently rapidly to prevent influences propagating around the system, but sufficiently slowly to avoid creating localized excitations. Compared to [7], the proof here is shorter and is generalized to systems at general filling fraction ρ\rho instead of just spin systems with total Sz=0S^{z}=0. It also explicitly constructs the low energy states for certain systems. Later, we discuss under what conditions these states can be identified as topological excitations.

Definition of System— We consider systems defined on a lattice, using letters i,j,…i,j,... to denote lattice sites (throughout, the term “site” may also be used to refer to a unit cell comprised of several sites), and introducing a metric d⁡(i,j)d(i,j) on the lattice. We assume that there is a conserved charge, Q=∑iQiQ=\sum_{i}Q_{i}, where QiQ_{i}, the charge on site ii, is quantized to be an integer (for example, QiQ_{i} may be taken to be the number of particles on a site, or in a spin system of half-integer spins QiQ_{i} may be equal to Siz+1/2S^{z}_{i}+1/2). We assume that the Hamiltonian, ℋ{\cal H} can be written as ℋ=∑iℋi{\cal H}=\sum_{i}{\cal H}^{i}, where the ℋi{\cal H}^{i} obey the finite range conditions[8, 9]: (1)(1) the commutator [ℋi,O]=0[{\cal H}^{i},O]=0 for any operator OO which acts only on sites jj with d⁡(i,j)>Rd(i,j)>R where RR is the range of the Hamiltonian; and (2)(2) the operator norm ‖ℋi‖≤J||{\cal H}^{i}||\leq J for all ii, for some constant JJ. Finally, the number of sites jj with d⁡(i,j)≤Rd(i,j)\leq R should be bounded by some number that we denote SS. These finite range conditions include all short-range boson systems with a finite number of bosons allowed per site, as well as all short-range spin systems.

We suppose that there are a total of VV sites on the dd-dimensional lattice. We assume that the Hamiltonian is translationally invariant in one of the directions of the lattice, with period LL: this is the length of the system. We define the filling fraction of the system to be ρ=Q/V\rho=Q/V. For each site ii, we introduce coordinates (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) to specify sites, where xix_{i} labels the distance along the length direction and yiy_{i} labels the transverse directions. The coordinate xx is periodic with period LL and should be compatible with the metric d⁡(i,j)d(i,j): any two sites i,ji,j should have d⁡(i,j)d(i,j) greater than or equal to the minimum over integers nn of |xi−xj−n​L||x_{i}-x_{j}-nL|.

We also define a twisted Hamiltonian and a rotation operator. Let

R⁡(θ)=∏j,0<xj≤L/2exp⁡[i​θ​(Qj−ρ)],R(\theta)=\prod_{j,0<x_{j}\leq L/2}\exp[i\theta(Q_{j}-\rho)], (1)

where the product ranges over all sites jj such that 0<xj≤L/20<x_{j}\leq L/2. We introduce two boundary condition twists as follows. Let ℋθ1,θ2=∑iℋθ1,θ2i{\cal H}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}=\sum_{i}{\cal H}^{i}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}, where ℋθ1,θ2i=R⁡(θ1)​ℋi​R​(−θ1){\cal H}^{i}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}=R(\theta_{1}){\cal H}^{i}R(-\theta_{1}) if −R≤xi≤R-R\leq x_{i}\leq R and ℋθ1,θ2i=R⁡(−θ2)​ℋi​R​(θ2){\cal H}^{i}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}=R(-\theta_{2}){\cal H}^{i}R(\theta_{2}) if L/2−R≤xi≤L/2+RL/2-R\leq x_{i}\leq L/2+R and otherwise ℋθ1,θ2i=ℋi{\cal H}^{i}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}={\cal H}^{i}. Thus, angle θ1\theta_{1} defines a twist in boundary conditions between x=0x=0 and x=1x=1, while angle θ2\theta_{2} defines a twist between x=L/2x=L/2 and x=L/2+1x=L/2+1. These twists correspond to inserting gauge flux between x=0x=0 and x=1x=1 or between x=L/2x=L/2 and x=L/2+1x=L/2+1. Let there be a total of NcN_{c} sites ii with −R≤xi≤R-R\leq x_{i}\leq R, and let ‖∂θℋθ1,θ2i‖≤K||\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}^{i}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}||\leq K for all ii for some constant KK. For a dd dimensional system with linear size LL and aspect ratio close to unity, Nc∼Ld−1N_{c}\sim L^{d-1}.

Let Ψ0​(θ1,θ2)\Psi_{0}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) be the ground state of ℋθ1,θ2{\cal H}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}, and let Ψ0\Psi_{0} be the ground state of ℋ0,0=ℋ{\cal H}_{0,0}={\cal H}. Note that ℋθ1,θ2=R⁡(−θ2)​ℋθ1+θ2,0​R​(θ2){\cal H}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}=R(-\theta_{2}){\cal H}_{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2},0}R(\theta_{2}) and in particular ℋθ,−θ=R⁡(θ)​ℋ​R​(−θ){\cal H}_{\theta,-\theta}=R(\theta){\cal H}R(-\theta) and Ψ0​(θ,−θ)=R⁡(θ)​Ψ0\Psi_{0}(\theta,-\theta)=R(\theta)\Psi_{0}. The second boundary condition angle thus appears to be redundant, since it is only the sum of the two angles, θ1+θ2\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}, that affects the eigenspectrum of ℋθ1,θ2{\cal H}_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}}. That is, the physical properties depend only on the total gauge flux θ1+θ2\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}. However, the introduction of the second boundary angle will be extremely useful below.

Results— The main result is that for a short-range Hamiltonian as defined above we are able to construct topologically excited states under certain assumptions on the spectrum of the Hamiltonian. The topologically excited states have a low energy but momentum that differs from the ground state momentum as given in Eq. (4,5,6). We begin by specifying the conditions on the spectrum.

Suppose that, for θ1=θ2=0\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}=0, there is a gap Δ​E\Delta E in energy between the ground state and a set of eigenstates, that we refer to as local excitations; we define Ph​i​g​hP_{high} to be the projection operator onto this space of states. There may be other eigenstates with energy below this gap; we define Pl​o​w=1−Ph​i​g​hP_{low}=1-P_{high} to project onto this space. We assume that for certain local operators OO, namely O=∂θℋθ,−θO=\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{\theta,-\theta} and O=∂θR⁡(θ)O=\partial_{\theta}R(\theta), the matrix elements of these operators, between Ψ0\Psi_{0} and any other normalized state Ψ\Psi which is a linear combination of eigenstates below the gap and which is orthogonal to the ground state, are bounded by ϵ​‖O‖\epsilon||O|| for some small constant ϵ\epsilon. Physically, we are interested in this case because in many situations the matrix elements of local operators between the ground state and topologically excited states are very small, often exponentially small in the system size. Since the Hamiltonian is translationally invariant, the ground state, Ψ0\Psi_{0}, may be taken translationally invariant, with eigenvalue z0z_{0}: T​Ψ0=z0​Ψ0T\Psi_{0}=z_{0}\Psi_{0} where TT is the translation operator which increases the xx-coordinate by 1.

One consequence of these results is a higher dimensional Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem for systems of with ρ⁡(V/L)\rho(V/L) non-integer, a case which includes spin systems with half-integer spin per unit cell, total Sz=0S^{z}=0, and odd width V/LV/L[7]. Discussion— The case of general filling fraction has been previously considered in one dimension, and used to study magnetization plateaus[10]. It was shown that gapped states could only exist at integer filling fraction, while at filling fraction ρ=p/q\rho=p/q with p,qp,q coprime there were found to be at least qq low energy states. We have shown very similar behavior in higher dimensions for ρ⁡(V/L)=p/q\rho(V/L)=p/q: if Δ​E\Delta E remains non-vanishing and ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 sufficiently rapidly as L→∞L\rightarrow\infty then we find that the states Ψn\Psi_{n}, for n=0,…,q−1n=0,...,q-1 provide qq degenerate low energy states. The nature of these qq states is not known a priori. They may correspond to either discrete symmetry breaking or to topological order. If all local operators, not just the specific ones considered in the proof above, have matrix elements between the low-lying states which vanish as L→∞L\rightarrow\infty, then we identify this as topological order. If some local operator has non-vanishing matrix elements between the local states, then there is long-range order in that operator[9], and we identify this as symmetry breaking. It is a limitation of the proof that the ability to construct low energy states depends on the width V/LV/L of the system. We conjecture that if ρ=p/q\rho=p/q then one can still find qq low lying states for arbitrary, sufficiently large, V/LV/L, but we are not able to prove this.

The technique shown in this paper is very general, and can be used in any case in which one can identify a quantized conserved charge, including cases of spins transforming under higher S​U​(N)SU(N) groups. Comparing to [11], the technique here creates a “global vison” excitation; if instead the flux is inserted along a finite line with endpoints, this technique can create a local “vison” excitation in two-dimensional spin systems as will be discussed elsewhere.
